<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads

  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }

  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S5" title="In SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">V </span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Experiments</span></span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_section">

<div class="ltx_page_main">

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line ltx_pruned_first">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation </h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jincheng Wang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Lingfan Bao
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tong Yang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Diego Martinez Plasencia
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jianhao Jiao<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Dimitrios Kanoulas
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The challenge of generating reliable local plans has long hindered practical applications in highly cluttered and dynamic environments. Key fundamental bottlenecks include acquiring large-scale expert demonstrations across diverse scenes and improving learning efficiency with limited data. This paper proposes SanD-Planner, a sample-efficient diffusion-based local planner that conducts depth image-based imitation learning within the clamped B-spline space. By operating within this compact space, the proposed algorithm inherently yields smooth outputs with bounded prediction errors over local supports, naturally aligning with receding-horizon execution. Integration of an ESDF-based safety checker with explicit clearance and time-to-completion metrics further reduces the training burden associated with value-function learning for feasibility assessment. Experiments show that training with <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>500</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">500</annotation></semantics></math> episodes (merely <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.25\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.25\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the demonstration scale used by the baseline), SanD-Planner achieves state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated open benchmark, attaining success rates of <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90.1\%</annotation></semantics></math> in simulated cluttered environments and <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="72.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>72.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">72.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> in indoor simulations. The performance is further proven by demonstrating zero-shot transferability to realistic experimentation in both 2D and 3D scenes. The dataset and pre-trained models will also be open-sourced.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="id2" class="ltx_logical-block">
    
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para"><img src="2602.00923v1/Images/First_figure.png" id="g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/143;" width="381" height="143" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
    
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Real-world demonstrations of SanD-Planner. Our method enables the robot to traverse cluttered environments with tight clearances, including navigating narrow passages, avoiding obstacles, and climbing stairs.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
  
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Corresponding author. <span id="footnotex1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">jianhao.jiao@ucl.ac.uk</span> The authors are with the Department of Computer Science, University College London.</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The capability for robust navigation in cluttered and dynamic environments remains a fundamental challenge for general-purpose mobile robotics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. Classic navigation frameworks typically utilize a modular pipeline that sequentially executes perception, SLAM, and planning sub-routines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>.
While effective in structured settings, the reliance on precise mapping creates bottlenecks in dynamic environments. Furthermore, the sequential processing induces latency and compounds errors from sensor noise and drift, often compromising the system’s ability to safely adapt to abrupt changes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This has catalyzed a shift toward end-to-end navigation approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> that map onboard observations directly to actions or trajectories. While deep reinforcement learning (DRL) provides a principled framework for policy acquisition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, it is often hindered by extreme sample inefficiency and the difficulty of reward engineering.
In contrast, imitation learning (IL) bypasses these issues by learning directly from expert demonstrations.
Recent advances have shown remarkable results by aggregating large-scale real-world datasets to achieve general navigation behaviors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. However, the success of these methods remains largely data-driven, relying heavily on the coverage and diversity of demonstrations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. This scaling trend highlights a common pattern: performance improvements often hinge on the expansion of the supervision pipeline rather than on learning effectively from limited data. In specific domains such as marine robotics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, this data scarcity is particularly difficult to overcome.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While scaling IL with massive datasets has driven remarkable progress, it often entails substantial computational overhead and longer training cycles. In this paper, we explore a complementary direction by asking whether local navigation can achieve high performance in a “data desert” of limited expert demonstrations.
We propose <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SanD-Planner</span>, a <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sa</span>mple-Efficie<span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">n</span>t <span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">D</span>iffusion-based Local <span id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Planner</span> that maps depth observations directly to smooth and parametric paths.
Unlike waypoint-based methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> that scale the output dimension linearly with the planning horizon, SanD-Planner predicts a fixed set of eight B-spline control points. This representation embeds structural geometric priors as an inductive bias, enabling an extended horizon to mitigate myopic behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> without increasing learning complexity.
By construction, B-splines ensure <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> continuity, making smoothness an inherent property rather than a learned feature. Crucially, the local support of B-splines provides robustness against the perceptual uncertainty typical of long-range sensing; noise or occlusions in the far horizon are isolated to distal control points, preventing far-field instabilities from propagating to the immediate execution segment.
Finally, we decouple trajectory generation from safety assessment via an interpretable online critic. By relegating feasibility checks to this explicit geometric module, we reduce learning complexity and allow the policy to focus exclusively on distilling the expert trajectory distribution. The contributions can be summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SanD-Planner</span>: A sample-efficient, diffusion-based local planner that generates smooth, collision-avoiding paths within a clamped cubic B-spline control-point space. By leveraging this structured representation, it achieves high-performance point-goal navigation using only <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">500</span> expert trajectories, which is <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 0.25\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 0.25\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the demonstration scale required by current state-of-the-art (SoTA) baselines.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Representation Study</span>: A systematic investigation conducted under a unified training and evaluation protocol, characterizing how trajectory representations, specifically discrete waypoints, interpolating cubic splines, and B-spline control points, impact the performance and sample efficiency of imitation learning-based local planners.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Validation</span>: Successful deployment on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot across diverse real-world environments, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. This demonstrates robust, depth-only 3D navigation in unseen complex scenes without any real-world fine-tuning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reproducibility</span>: We will release our complete training and evaluation framework, including the dataset and pre-trained models, upon the acceptance.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Related Work</span></h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">II-A</span> </span><span id="S2.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Learning-based End-to-End Visual Navigation</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DRL is a prominent category in this domain, employing trial-and-error optimization to eliminate the need for labeled data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. However, DRL is notoriously sample-inefficient and relies on complex reward engineering that often proves more difficult than providing expert demonstrations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. IL has emerged as a practical paradigm, enabling policies to learn directly from expert behaviors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. Building on this foundation, recent approaches have explored generative policy (<span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.,</span> diffusion policy) learning to model local paths as conditional distributions, capturing the inherent multi-modality of navigation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.
However, the robustness of IL policies is fundamentally constrained by the diversity and long-tail coverage of training data, especially in complex geometric configurations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. Consequently, pushing the limits of end-to-end navigation has largely depended on scaling expert demonstrations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. This is typically achieved by aggregating large real-world datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> or by generating high-quality simulation supervision at scale, rather than learning effectively from limited data. For instance, recent works such as NavDP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> leverage high-fidelity simulators to generate extensive supervision, utilizing datasets spanning hundreds of kilometers and requiring substantial compute budgets.
In contrast to the trend of data scaling, this work demonstrates that a robust local planning policy can be learned effectively with limited data by injecting structural priors. We leverage B-spline parameterization to explicitly enforce path smoothness and inherent representation-level robustness. By combining this generative policy with an explicit geometric critic for trajectory selection, we decouple safety verification from policy learning. This design enables robust navigation with significantly fewer demonstrations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">II-B</span> </span><span id="S2.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B-spline Representation in Navigation</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">B-splines are standard trajectory representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> in motion planning, where optimizing in a compact control-point space enables efficiency under smoothness and feasibility constraints. Classical optimization-based planners exploit spline structures, such as the convex-hull property, to improve clearance and dynamic feasibility <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>. These results suggest that trajectory parameterization can serve as a powerful inductive bias for learning-based navigation.
In previous works, many IL policies were supervised using single-step actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, making temporal consistency an explicit learning burden <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>. To mitigate this, recent planners predict short-horizon waypoint rollouts or action sequences to encourage coherent motion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>. Moving beyond discrete sequences, recent approaches predict sparse waypoints and convert them into cubic-spline paths <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. In contrast, this work learns local planning directly in a clamped B-spline control-point space, thereby inheriting the continuity and convex-hull properties. Our analysis (Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="IV-B Trajectory Parameterization via B-Spline Control Points ‣ IV Methodology ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B</span></a>) has demonstrated that B-splines offer distinct advantages for imitation-based planners compared to waypoint or standard cubic-spline parameterizations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.00923v1/Images/overview_new.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/117;" width="452" height="117" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of SanD-Planner.<span id="S2.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The pipeline tokenizes and fuses historical depth images, relative point goals, and previous velocity using a two-layer Transformer encoder. The multi-modal context conditions a diffusion policy to generate B-spline control points through iterative denoising. Finally, an geometric critic module selects the optimal plan from candidates for execution and feeds its initial velocity back to the next planning step to maintain temporal consistency.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Problem Formulation</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work addresses mapless local navigation in cluttered environments by learning a collision-free goal-reaching policy. At each planning step <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the robot receives a short history of four depth images <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}_{t}=\{\mathbf{D}_{t-3},\mathbf{D}_{t-2},\mathbf{D}_{t-1},\mathbf{D}_{t}\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}_{t}=\{\mathbf{D}_{t-3},\mathbf{D}_{t-2},\mathbf{D}_{t-1},\mathbf{D}_{t}\},</annotation></semantics></math> captured in the robot frame, and receives a three-dimensional relative goal <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{t}=[x,y,z]^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{t}=[x,y,z]^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> expressed in the same frame. To ensure temporal consistency across consecutive replanning cycles, we also incorporate a motion context term <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{prev}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>prev</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{prev}}</annotation></semantics></math> that encodes the heading direction of the plan executed in the previous step. These inputs are projected via domain-specific encoders <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{(\cdot)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{(\cdot)}</annotation></semantics></math> and fused into a unified latent context
<math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}=\Phi\Big(f_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{O}_{t}),\,f_{g}(\mathbf{g}_{t}),\,f_{v}(\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{prev}})\Big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>prev</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}=\Phi\Big(f_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{O}_{t}),\,f_{g}(\mathbf{g}_{t}),\,f_{v}(\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{prev}})\Big)</annotation></semantics></math> using an encoder <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>. Instead of predicting waypoint sequences, our planner operates in the structured space of B-spline control points. We parameterize each output local trajectory <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> as a sequence of <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> control points <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}_{t}=\{\mathbf{Q}_{t,i}\}_{i=0}^{N-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}_{t}=\{\mathbf{Q}_{t,i}\}_{i=0}^{N-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math> in the robot frame.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The objective is to generate a smooth, collision-free trajectory <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> that efficiently connects the current pose to <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. To this end, we learn a conditional diffusion model <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\theta}(\mathcal{Q}_{t}\mid\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}(\mathcal{Q}_{t}\mid\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> from expert demonstrations that captures the distribution of feasible control points. During planning, the diffusion policy samples <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> candidate control-point sets <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{Q}^{(k)}_{t}\}_{k=1}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{Q}^{(k)}_{t}\}_{k=1}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, which generate continuous trajectories <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\bm{\tau_{t}}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝒕</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mmultiscripts><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\bm{\tau_{t}}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math>. The optimal plan <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}_{t}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}_{t}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is then selected from these candidates by minimizing a task-specific cost <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>, which encompasses safety constraints and efficiency.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Methodology</span></h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S2.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ II-B B-spline Representation in Navigation ‣ II Related Work ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, SanD-Planner presents a two-stage generate-and-select pipeline:
<span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1)</span> trajectory generation within a B-spline control-point space (Sections <a href="#S4.SS2" title="IV-B Trajectory Parameterization via B-Spline Control Points ‣ IV Methodology ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B</span></a>–<a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Diffusion Policy for Local Trajectory Generation ‣ IV Methodology ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a>), and
<span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2)</span> critic-based selection with explicit geometric objectives (Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="IV-D Safety-Aware Candidate Selection via the Critic Module ‣ IV Methodology ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-D</span></a>).
In the first stage, the policy network uses a conditional diffusion model to sample <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> candidate control-point sets <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math> conditioned on the context tensor <math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Subsequently, these discrete sets are mapped to continuous local trajectories via B-spline basis functions. In the second stage, a lightweight ESDF-based critic module ranks these candidates by evaluating a task-specific cost function. The trajectory with the lowest cost, <math id="S4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}_{t}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}_{t}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, is selected as the local plan and executed in a receding-horizon manner. The initial heading velocity of the selected trajectory is fed back as <math id="S4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{prev}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>prev</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{prev}}</annotation></semantics></math> to condition the next planning step.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-A</span> </span><span id="S4.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Perception and Condition Encoding</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At each planning step <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the agent receives historical observations <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to capture environmental dynamics. Each depth frame is encoded using a lightweight ResNet-18 backbone <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\mathcal{O}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\mathcal{O}}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>. To preserve fine-grained geometric details essential for local obstacle avoidance (<span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.,</span> obstacle edges or stair steps), we extract spatial feature maps <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times D}</annotation></semantics></math> for each frame from an intermediate layer rather than the final layer. These spatial features <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐅</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{F}</annotation></semantics></math> are then flattened into a sequence of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\times W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\times W</annotation></semantics></math> visual tokens. To maintain spatial and temporal structure, we augment each token with 2D positional embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> and a learnable temporal embedding to distinguish tokens from different time steps. The resulting visual embedding sequence is denoted as <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}_{\mathcal{O}}=f_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{O}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times(HW)\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}_{\mathcal{O}}=f_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{O}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times(HW)\times D}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Simultaneously, we project the relative goal <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and the previously executed velocity <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{prev}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>prev</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{prev}}</annotation></semantics></math> into the same latent dimension <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> via dedicated Multi-Layer Perceptrons, serving as encoders <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{v}</annotation></semantics></math>. This yields the goal token <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}_{g}=f_{g}(\mathbf{g}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}_{g}=f_{g}(\mathbf{g}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> and the velocity token <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}_{v}=f_{v}(\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{prev}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>prev</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}_{v}=f_{v}(\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\mathrm{prev}})</annotation></semantics></math>. If historical velocity is unavailable (<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.,</span> <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0</annotation></semantics></math>), a learnable null token substitutes <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}_{v}</annotation></semantics></math>. All tokens are then concatenated into a sequence and aggregated by a two-layer Transformer encoder <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>. The final output serves as the multi-modal context <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}=\Phi([\mathbf{e}_{\mathcal{O}},\mathbf{e}_{g},\mathbf{e}_{v}])" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>v</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}=\Phi([\mathbf{e}_{\mathcal{O}},\mathbf{e}_{g},\mathbf{e}_{v}])</annotation></semantics></math>, which is subsequently used to condition the diffusion denoising process.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Trajectory Parameterization via B-Spline Control Points</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We represent each trajectory as a clamped cubic B-spline which inherently possesses <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> continuity to ensure its smoothness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.
Given a B-spline of degree <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> and a set of knot vectors <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}=\{{u}_{0},\dots,{u}_{N+p}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}=\{{u}_{0},\dots,{u}_{N+p}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, the trajectory <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as</p>
<table id="S4.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}_{t}(u)\;=\;\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}B_{i,p}(u)\,\mathbf{Q}_{t,i},\qquad u\in[u_{p},u_{N}]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.391em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}_{t}(u)\;=\;\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}B_{i,p}(u)\,\mathbf{Q}_{t,i},\qquad u\in[u_{p},u_{N}],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{i,p}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{i,p}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> are the B-spline basis functions.
We employ a uniform knot vector, anchoring the curve at the endpoints so that <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}_{t}({u}_{p})=\mathbf{Q}_{t,0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}_{t}({u}_{p})=\mathbf{Q}_{t,0}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}_{t}({u}_{N})=\mathbf{Q}_{t,N-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}_{t}({u}_{N})=\mathbf{Q}_{t,N-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The control points <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are defined in the robot frame, hence <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}_{t,0}=\mathbf{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟎</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}_{t,0}=\mathbf{0}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This parameterization transforms the learning objective from a discrete sequence of waypoints to a compact set of control points.
To characterize the efficacy of the B-spline representation, we contrast its structured geometric priors against two prevalent IL parameterizations: discrete waypoints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> and interpolating cubic splines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> in the following content.
As illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV-B Trajectory Parameterization via B-Spline Control Points ‣ IV Methodology ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, these representations exhibit differences regarding parameter compactness and inherent robustness to perceptual noise. We then discuss three advantages of B-spline parameterization with toy examples:</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of trajectory representations among discrete waypoints, cubic spline, and B-spline.
(a) Ground-truth A* path (gray) and an 8-waypoint sequence (orange, <math id="S4.F3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.2m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.2m</annotation></semantics></math> spacing).
(b) Mean arc-length displacement <math id="S4.F3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta(s)</annotation></semantics></math> under identical perturbations (<math id="S4.F3.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\times</annotation></semantics></math> disturbances). Over the first <math id="S4.F3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5m</annotation></semantics></math>, the B-spline deviation stays near zero, whereas the cubic spline oscillates.
(c, d) We first fit the same ground-truth path with an 8-point interpolating cubic spline (c) and an <math id="S4.F3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math>-point B-spline (d), and then apply the random perturbations to the last four points within a <math id="S4.F3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1m</annotation></semantics></math> radius. Owing to local support and convex hull property, B-splines avoid overshoot and better preserve the global path shape, yielding smaller deviations than cubic splines under the same perturbation range.
</span></figcaption><img src="2602.00923v1/Images/FIgure3.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:452/404;" width="452" height="404" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span>1 </span>Parameter Efficiency</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV-B Trajectory Parameterization via B-Spline Control Points ‣ IV Methodology ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(a) and (c), modeling trajectories with control points instead of dense waypoints yields a compact manifold that simplifies the diffusion process without sacrificing expressivity. Crucially, B-splines facilitate long-horizon planning within a fixed-dimensional output space, effectively avoiding the myopia issues often encountered in traditional methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span>2 </span>Smoothness as Inductive Bias</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Cubic B-splines are <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-continuous, ensuring smooth position, velocity, and acceleration profiles. Critically, this smoothness is a structural property of the representation rather than a feature learned from data. By predicting control points, the policy is constrained to output smooth trajectories even when trained on limited or noisy expert demonstrations, thereby simplifying the learning objective and enhancing trackability for downstream control.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span>3 </span>Representation-Level Robustness</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Depth sensing often suffers from partial, noisy observations and occlusions, which compromise the reliability of long-range planning. B-splines offer representation-level robustness against this issue through two key properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Local Support:</span> A B-spline segment depends only on <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p+1</annotation></semantics></math> local control points. Consequently, noise-induced deviations in distal control points remain isolated and do not reshape the entire path. This property aligns naturally with receding-horizon planning, allowing the robot to execute a stable near-horizon segment while iteratively correcting far-horizon errors in subsequent steps. In contrast, globally coupled interpolating splines propagate local perturbations across the entire trajectory, potentially destabilizing immediate actions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Convex Hull Property:</span> To ensure safety under distribution shifts, the representation should prevent prediction errors from amplifying into large path deviations. Since B-spline basis functions <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{i,p}(u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{i,p}(u)</annotation></semantics></math> satisfy the partition of unity (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e.,</span> <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum B_{i,p}(u)=1,B_{i,p}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>∑</mo><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum B_{i,p}(u)=1,B_{i,p}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math>), every point on the trajectory <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau}_{t}(u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau}_{t}(u)</annotation></semantics></math> lies within the convex hull of its control points. For a predicted set with errors <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}^{\prime}_{t,i}=\mathbf{Q}_{t,i}+\Delta\mathbf{Q}_{t,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}^{\prime}_{t,i}=\mathbf{Q}_{t,i}+\Delta\mathbf{Q}_{t,i}</annotation></semantics></math>, the trajectory deviation is uniformly bounded by the maximum control-point error:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{u}\bigl\|\bm{\tau}^{\prime}_{t}(u)-\bm{\tau}_{t}(u)\bigr\|\leq\max_{i}\bigl\|\Delta\mathbf{Q}_{t,i}\bigr\|." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>u</mi></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>i</mi></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐐</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{u}\bigl\|\bm{\tau}^{\prime}_{t}(u)-\bm{\tau}_{t}(u)\bigr\|\leq\max_{i}\bigl\|\Delta\mathbf{Q}_{t,i}\bigr\|.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Eq. (<a href="#S4.E2" title="In IV-B3 Representation-Level Robustness ‣ IV-B Trajectory Parameterization via B-Spline Control Points ‣ IV Methodology ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) shows that B-splines prevent error amplification by providing a strict upper bound on path deviation. As shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV-B Trajectory Parameterization via B-Spline Control Points ‣ IV Methodology ‣ SanD-Planner: Sample-Efficient Diffusion Planner in B-Spline Space for Robust Local Navigation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, B-splines preserve the global trajectory shape even under perturbation, whereas interpolating splines often suffer from Runge’s phenomenon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, where small nodal errors induce disproportionately large overshoots.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Diffusion Policy for Local Trajectory Generation</span></h3>

<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span>1 </span>Diffusion in B-Spline Control-Point Space</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We model local planning as conditional generation in B-spline control-point space. Given the conditioning context <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the generator samples a set of control points <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is deterministically mapped to a continuous trajectory <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\tau_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝉</mi><mi>𝒕</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\tau_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math> via the B-spline representation.
Let <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\mathcal{\mathbf{Q}}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐐</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\mathcal{\mathbf{Q}}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the expert control points obtained by fitting a B-spline to an expert trajectory, and let <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}:=\mathrm{vec}(\bar{\mathcal{\mathbf{Q}}}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>vec</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐐</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}:=\mathrm{vec}(\bar{\mathcal{\mathbf{Q}}}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> be the corresponding clean control-point vector. We train a conditional DDPM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> to model <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathcal{C}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathcal{C}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>. With a predefined noise schedule <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(\alpha_{s},\sigma_{s})\}_{s=1}^{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>S</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(\alpha_{s},\sigma_{s})\}_{s=1}^{S}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{s}^{2}+\sigma_{s}^{2}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{s}^{2}+\sigma_{s}^{2}=1</annotation></semantics></math>, the forward process is</p>
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})=\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\alpha_{s}\mathbf{x}_{0},\ \sigma_{s}^{2}\mathbf{I}\bigr),\qquad s\in\{1,\ldots,S\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.798em;" width="0.798em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\mathbf{x}_{s}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})=\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\alpha_{s}\mathbf{x}_{0},\ \sigma_{s}^{2}\mathbf{I}\bigr),\qquad s\in\{1,\ldots,S\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the total number of denoising steps and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> is the current diffusion step. We employ the <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>-prediction parameterization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> with the target defined as <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{s}:=\alpha_{s}\bm{\epsilon}-\sigma_{s}\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{s}:=\alpha_{s}\bm{\epsilon}-\sigma_{s}\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})</annotation></semantics></math>. A denoiser is trained to predict the diffusion target conditioned on the context embedding and timestep.
Specifically, we use a conditional 1D U-Net over the control-point sequence with cross-attention to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and timestep embeddings injected into each block, and predict the <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>-parameterization target <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{v}}=\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{s},\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t},s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{v}}=\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{s},\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t},s)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The training objective is the standard <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>-prediction loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite></p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\bm{\epsilon},s}\Bigl[\bigl\|\mathbf{v}_{s}-\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{c}_{t},s)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\bm{\epsilon},s}\Bigl[\bigl\|\mathbf{v}_{s}-\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{s},\mathbf{c}_{t},s)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">During inference, given <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{c}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{c}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we initialize the diffusion process from Gaussian noise and run <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> reverse denoising steps to sample <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> candidate B-spline control-point sets <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{(k)}\sim p_{\theta}(\mathcal{Q}_{t}\mid\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓒</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{(k)}\sim p_{\theta}(\mathcal{Q}_{t}\mid\bm{\mathcal{C}}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in\{1,\dots,K\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo
